anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (memory, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, causing secondary performance pathologies even though the physical resources are not inherently exhausted.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots inside the buffer manager, producing buffer-busy waits, CPU spin, and latency spikes driven by page-level contention rather than total memory shortage.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply redo at the rate generated on the primary, leading to widening log gaps, replay lag, and retention of un-recycled log segments.

Composite behaviour: When mis-tuned configuration parameters simultaneously foster buffer-cache/latch hot spots and accelerate redo generation, the primary instance experiences both severe page-level contention and a surge in transaction-log traffic that replicas fail to keep up with. Observable symptoms include: 1) mixed wait-event spikes—buffer-busy, page-latch, log-flush, and replication-sender waits—cycling in unpredictable patterns; 2) CPU utilisation that oscillates between spin-loops on latches and idle periods while replication back-pressure throttles commit throughput; 3) bloating of the primary’s transaction log because replication prevents recycling while aggressive checkpoints keep forcing additional flushes; 4) replica-side apply workers falling further behind, showing elevated lock conflicts on the same hotspot pages once they finally replay, and 5) end-user latency outliers that are hard to attribute to a single tier because stalls propagate from buffer manager to commit path to replication pipeline.

Causal chain: Poor configuration—for example an undersized buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint interval, or improper work-memory/granule sizing—magnifies page churn and concentrates traffic on a limited set of cache lines. This intensifies latch contention, which lengthens commit time and inflates the volume and burstiness of redo writes. The heavier, more bursty log stream in turn overwhelms replicas, introducing apply lag that blocks log truncation on the primary. Retained log segments consume more cache and I/O bandwidth, further shrinking effective buffer space and prolonging dirty-page residence, which feeds back into even higher latch contention cycles. Thus, each anomaly amplifies the others: mis-tuned parameters create the hot pages, latch contention slows commit, slow commits inflate log backlog, and replication drag prevents cleanup, together degrading both primary and replica performance far beyond what any single issue would cause.

entry.official_definition: Aborts any statement that waits longer than the specified amount of time while attempting to acquire a lock.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_timeout for a table, index, row, or other database object lock.
entry.workload_impact: The statement attempting to acquire the lock is aborted.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
